screens.title: Exploit probe: reweight sampled worlds by self-model
screens.candidate: exploitability probe (#625 step 4): the belief-reweighting ATTACKER -- the served release-30/31 policy with the world prior reweighted by per-decision log-likelihoods (arm identity ...-exploit-7c602a04a)
screens.comparator: the same package with the reweighting short-circuited at floor>=1, i.e. served parity (arm identity ...-exploit-2f5e6c244)
screens.vs_group: the same package, exploit reweighting off (release 30 era)
screens.instrument: twenty 520-cluster mirrored windows (10,400 deal-pairs), 300 s cap, arms interleaved per seed; DL random effects; PRE-REGISTERED at 20 windows / MDE80 0.0255 with one interim look at the VARIANCE only
screens.takeaway: Inconclusive; later judged a flawed probe (self-model, two cards of evidence), so it says nothing about exploitability or any bound.
screens.note: METHOD CORRECTION (Jerry 09-26, 'it doesn't make sense MC-LCB is not exploitable' -- he was right): this run does NOT bear on MC-LCB's exploitability. The attacker's belief model is a SELF-model -- P(opponent played X | world) is scored with the attacker's OWN policy head, so it never models MC-LCB or any specific opponent -- and it conditions only on the opposing team's plays in the CURRENT trick (at most two cards), discarding all prior tricks. Mechanical diagnostic on 6 self-play deals / 163 evidence-bearing decisions (Mini, not the screen; indicative only): the world weights do move (effective-sample-size ratio median 0.63, p10 0.30) but change the chosen action in only 8.6% of decisions. So the null is explained by a wrong opponent model, two cards of evidence and a ~50% tie rate -- not by MC-LCB being robust. The interval stands as a number; read 'this attack' as 'a self-model on two cards'. Whether MC-LCB, or anything, is exploitable by an attacker that models its opponent and uses the history is UNTESTED. THE PARTY EXPLOITED IS mc-s0-report-lcb, NOT the current served policy: the harness passes --baseline production and that name resolves to the release-28-era W32 play policy, two releases stale. So this reads as 'belief reweighting does not help a PV searcher beat MC-LCB more than a plain PV searcher does', and says nothing about how exploitable release 30/31 is as an opponent. The contrast is still valid -- both arms face the identical baseline. CROSSES ZERO -- inconclusive as to direction; the point estimate is NOT a finding that the attacker is worse. What this establishes is the UPPER BOUND the probe was designed for: any gain from this attack is at most +0.0109 per-round signed level utility at 95%, against a typical per-round utility of +0.13 to +0.19. MDE80 landed at 0.0255 against the pre-registered 0.0255, so the variance model was right; tau 0, I2 0.0%, Q 14.11/19df. All 40 windows complete, 0 refused, arm identities confirmed distinct. COST: attacker decision latency p95 0.80 s vs control 0.15 s (max 2.13 vs 1.02) for no detected gain. Tie rate 49.5% vs 50.0% -- close, but these are rounded means and are not being called identical. This bounds THIS attacker, not exploitability in general. Recomputed with fl-pilot/vol_re.py and archived at ~/shengji-archive/2026-09-13/readouts/x36a-exploit-vs-control/ with SHA256SUMS.

Reweighting a fixed 64 worlds by a deterministic opponent's eps-smoothed likelihood over ~20 observed plays collapses the posterior onto ~3 worlds (ESS ratio median 0.048 in the #647 smoke) that mismatched least -- confident and wrong -- and the value head then scores over three noisy worlds. NOTHING about SmartBot's or MC-LCB's exploitability follows; x36a's null was a milder dose of the same instrument and is no longer readable as a bound. A working instrument needs evidence-conditioned SAMPLING (keep N surviving worlds) or a tempered, ESS-floored likelihood that refuses to reweight below the floor, validated on the smoke (ESS >= ~0.5 and a head-alone win vs SmartBot) before any lane. mc-lite / production / shortlist runs are OFF until then. Both arms are the same class over the same package; this is a same-window paired contrast of the belief floor, not a strength screen.

models_note: The gen-4 runs are ONE experiment, not four models: the same corpus (all 20 stores, 336,000 deals) and the same evaluation, with a small number of ingredients changed per run. The numbers are the plan's order, not the order they ran — Jerry reordered execution to 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 on 2026-09-21 so the objective was tested before depth. Run 1 is the baseline: gen-3-warm's recipe (residual trunk d4, JS-M1 warm start) on the bigger corpus with HARD targets, the played action as the policy label. Run 4 changes exactly one thing against it, the objective: SOFT targets, the search's own per-candidate values. Runs 2 and 3 are ALSO soft, so the reference for them is RUN 4, not run 1: run 2 changes capacity (residual trunk at depth 6 instead of 4) and run 3 changes architecture AND warm start together (a grid trunk, depth 3 and 44 channels, started from JS-G1 instead of JS-M1). So run 1 vs run 4 isolates the objective, run 4 vs run 2 isolates depth, and run 4 vs run 3 moves two things at once — which is why run 3's read is not attributable to a single ingredient.
head_ladder_note: Policy head ALONE: each head plays every card decision by argmax of its summed card log-odds over the capped legal set, no value net, no rollouts, heuristic declare/bury, 8,000 mirrored deals (seed0 20000, the 09-18 ladder's harness). 'vs SmartBot' is the ladder; 'vs production head' is a PAIRED duel of two heads on the same deals, the release-30 head (8ecd4fea) scored by the identical rule (its self-duel reads exactly 0). Standard for every exported model from 2026-09-30. These measure the admission head alone; the served search (which the value head decides) is what the screens read. A better head alone is not a better served bot: PBF1 reads +0.238 vs the production head (paired vs SMV3 +0.031 [+0.015,+0.048]) yet served v39a reads -0.0525 [-0.0878,-0.0171] vs release 36.
